claims.text: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in the stated homogeneous single-phase state has low hardness and strength.
The homogeneous single-phase solid solution lacks significant dislocation obstacles.
The alloy has low inherent lattice distortion.
The alloy lacks significant short-range ordering.
The starting alloy lacks secondary-phase precipitates.
The homogeneous single-phase alloy permits rapid dynamic recovery.
The absence of obstacles and rapid dynamic recovery favor easy planar dislocation glide with minimal dislocation accumulation.
Minimal dislocation accumulation limits forest hardening and work hardening.
Limited obstacle strengthening and work hardening govern the low hardness and yield strength of the starting alloy.
Controlled aging can induce nanoscale precipitates in equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
Nanoscale precipitates create barriers to dislocation motion and increase dislocation pinning.
The precipitate-strengthened variant will have statistically significantly greater yield strength and hardness than the as-cast alloy.
The precipitate-strengthened variant will show increased dislocation impediments, such as higher dislocation density or localized lattice strain.
The precipitate-strengthened variant will retain relatively high overall ductility.
The proposed mechanism applies under room-temperature, quasi-static loading to equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi initially processed as a single-phase solid solution.
The mechanism may not apply under extreme strain-rate or temperature conditions.

contradictions.description: The intervention and predicted outcome require aging to create nanoscale precipitates, but the conditions state that testing preserves the single-phase state. A precipitate-bearing comparison specimen is not a single-phase specimen.

The boundary says the hypothesis may not apply when secondary phases are deliberately introduced, while the controlled comparison deliberately introduces precipitates and uses that state to test the proposed mechanism.
